## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

16	# R1 Review: Methods and Experiments
17	
18	**Paper**: "What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? A Systematic Study of Mining Strategies and Representation Geometry"
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Summary
23	
24	The paper presents a controlled comparison of three hard negative mining strategies (random, embedding-distance, dataflow-aware) for contrastive code retrieval, evaluated across two 3B-parameter encoders with 9 seeds each. The main findings are that embedding-distance mining consistently improves R@1 (+2.3pp Qwen, +1.7pp StarCoder), while dataflow-aware mining provides conditional benefit mediated by representation saturation (significant on Qwen, null on StarCoder). The experimental design is ambitious and the ablation suite is commendably broad, but several methodological concerns -- including the generalizability of the "representation geometry" theory from only 2 encoders, unrealistic retrieval pool sizes, missing baselines, and discrepancies between reported and actual result maturity -- undermine the strength of the claims.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Strengths
29	
30	- **Exemplary experimental scale and statistical discipline.** 54 training runs (2 x 3 x 9) with paired bootstrap 95% CIs and explicit p-values for all main comparisons is well above the standard for this subfield. The paper does not rely on single-seed results, and the statistical testing is appropriate (bootstrap CIs, paired comparisons).
31	
32	- **Comprehensive ablation suite with clear analytical purpose.** Each ablation (temperature, hop depth, data scaling, fusion head, static vs. dynamic mining, binary vs. weighted dataflow) answers a specific methodological question rather than padding the paper. The dynamic mining baseline (Table 13) is particularly valuable for ruling out curriculum effects as a confound, and the fusion head ablation (Table 11) cleanly separates training-time mining value from inference-time feature injection.
33	
34	- **Honest reporting of null and conditional results.** The StarCoder dataflow null (p=0.62), the dataflow-vs-embed non-significance (p=0.134 on SWE-bench), and the diminishing returns at scale (Table 10) are reported transparently. Many papers would suppress these findings.
35	
36	- **Mechanistically motivated analysis.** The representation saturation explanation (pos_sim 0.986 vs. 0.799) goes beyond "method X beats method Y" to provide a predictive framework. If validated, the pos_sim diagnostic could be a genuinely useful practitioner tool.
37	
38	- **Clean experimental control.** The comparison holds all variables constant except the negative selection strategy -- same data, same encoder, same LoRA configuration, same training schedule. This is the correct way to study the effect of a single factor.
39	
40	- **SWE-bench Lite end-to-end evaluation.** Including downstream task evaluation, even though the results are positive, adds credibility beyond retrieval-only metrics.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Weaknesses
45	
46	### Major
47	
48	1. **Generalizability from N=2 encoders is fundamentally limited (Section 5, Discussion).** The paper's central mechanistic claim -- that representation saturation mediates the effectiveness of structural negatives -- rests on exactly two data points: Qwen (saturated, pos_sim=0.986) and StarCoder (healthy, pos_sim=0.799). This is insufficient to establish a functional relationship. The two encoders also differ in pretraining data, pretraining objective, tokenizer, and model family, meaning the observed interaction could be driven by any of these confounds rather than representation geometry per se. The paper characterizes StarCoder2-3B as "encoder-decoder" (Section 3.4), but StarCoder2-3B is decoder-only (autoregressive), making the claimed "architecturally distinct" comparison misleading. At minimum, the paper needs (a) to correct the architectural characterization, and (b) to explicitly acknowledge that the saturation theory is an observation from N=2, not a validated mechanism.
49	
50	2. **Pool size of 50 candidates per query is unrealistically small (Section 3.4, implicitly).** Real-world repositories contain hundreds to thousands of files. A pool of 50 means the retriever is choosing among ~50 files, which inflates absolute recall numbers and may mask differences between strategies that would emerge at realistic pool sizes. The paper does not discuss this design choice or its implications for external validity. At pool=50, even random selection has a 2% baseline chance per candidate, making R@1 in the 0.50+ range less impressive. The RepoBench-R evaluation (Table 5) uses a different pool size but this is not specified.
51	
52	3. **Missing BM25 negative baseline.** The paper's headline narrative -- correcting CoCoHaNeRe's finding that embedding negatives harm code search -- attributes the prior result to BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance. Yet the paper never runs actual BM25 negatives to demonstrate that the harm is BM25-specific. This is the single most important missing experiment given the framing. Without it, the "correction" is argumentative rather than empirical.
53	
54	4. **SWE-bench Lite results appear inflated relative to project state.** The paper reports +2.3pp (embedding) and +3.3pp (dataflow) resolve-rate gains over random on SWE-bench Lite, with bootstrap CIs excluding zero (Table 4). However, training data from the project's internal decision log (D018, D019, D026, D027) shows that as of the review date, the full M2 runs (9 seeds per strategy per encoder) are still in progress, with only seed 1 partially completed for each encoder. The pilot results (D017) from 1 seed show much smaller effects (+2.0pp Qwen embedding, with dataflow ranking dependent on checkpoint selection criterion). The SWE-bench results reported in the "best" paper variant are substantially stronger than the evidence base supports. If these are projected/simulated results, this must be disclosed.
55	
56	5. **No error bars or CIs on RepoBench-R results (Table 5).** RepoBench-R results are reported as single numbers without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given that the reported deltas (e.g., +1.9pp R@1 for embedding on Qwen) are small, these may not be statistically distinguishable from zero. For a paper that emphasizes statistical rigor on the SWE-smith results, the asymmetry in reporting standards is conspicuous.
57	
58	6. **SWE-smith validation results mentioned but not shown.** Section 4 references SWE-smith validation R@1 as the primary evaluation metric, and the main tables (Tables 1-2) report these. But the actual validation set construction, size, and overlap with training data are not described. Given that the project logs show severe overfitting (best checkpoint at step 1000 out of 4242, D026), the validation protocol is critical for interpreting results, yet insufficiently documented.
59	
60	7. **34% structural coverage dilutes the dataflow signal (Section 3.3, implicit).** Only 34.3% of training instances receive dataflow-mined negatives; the remaining 65.7% fall back to alternative selection (presumably embedding or random). The reported +1.5pp dataflow improvement (Table 1, Qwen) averages over all instances including those that received no structural signal. Stratified results (structural-available vs. fallback) are absent. The true per-instance effect of dataflow mining on instances where it actually applies could be much larger (or much smaller) than the reported average. This stratification is essential for interpreting the result.
61	
62	### Minor
63	
64	8. **Table 6 "<50 instances" tier has N=1 repo.** Including a tier with a single repository is misleading and inflates the apparent trend. The correlation r=-0.41 (p=0.08) is heavily influenced by this outlier. The tier should either be removed or its N=1 status should be prominently flagged with appropriate caveats.
65	
66	9. **LoRA rank 16, 3 epochs may be insufficient.** With LoRA rank 16 (a low-rank adapter), the encoder's representational capacity to learn from different negative strategies is limited. Strategy differences might only emerge with fuller fine-tuning. The paper does not discuss whether LoRA's low-rank bottleneck could compress away the differences between strategies. The observed overfitting at step 1000 (1/4 through training) suggests the learning dynamics are dominated by regularization effects, not data effects.
67	
68	10. **Checkpoint selection criterion ambiguity.** The project history (D017) reveals that strategy rankings change depending on whether checkpoints are selected by best validation loss or best R@1. The paper does not specify which criterion is used. Given that this choice can reverse the ordering of strategies (dataflow > embedding by peak R@1 vs. embedding > dataflow by val_loss for Qwen, per D017), this is a material omission.
69	
70	11. **All references render as [?].** The bibliography is broken -- every citation in the compiled paper appears as [?]. This makes it impossible to verify the related work coverage or the CoCoHaNeRe critique. For a paper whose central claim involves correcting a prior work's methodology, unresolvable citations are a serious presentation issue.
71	
72	12. **Number of negatives per query (K) not stated.** The method section defines "select k negatives" but never specifies the value of K used in experiments. This is a basic reproducibility gap.
73	
74	13. **Overfitting patterns not reported.** Project logs show train_loss dropping to 0.04 while val_loss remains at 0.52 (D026), yet the paper does not discuss overfitting or show learning curves. Strategy-specific overfitting patterns could be informative (e.g., does dataflow overfit faster due to fewer unique negatives?).
75	
76	---
77	
78	## Questions for Authors
79	
80	1. **SWE-bench result provenance.** Tables 3-4 report SWE-bench Lite results with bootstrap CIs excluding zero for embedding and dataflow vs. random. Are these from completed 9-seed runs, or projected from pilot data? If the full M2 runs are still in progress, what is the actual evidence base for these numbers?
81	
82	2. **Checkpoint selection criterion.** Which checkpoint is used for the main results -- best by validation loss, or best by R@1? Your project logs (D017) show these criteria produce different strategy rankings. Have you reported both, and if not, why?
83	
84	3. **Stratified dataflow results.** What is the R@1 delta for the ~34% of instances that actually receive dataflow-mined negatives vs. the ~66% that fall back? This decomposition is essential for understanding whether the dataflow signal is strong-but-diluted or weak-throughout.
85	
86	4. **BM25 baseline omission.** The paper's narrative hinges on CoCoHaNeRe using "BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance." Can you provide specific textual evidence from CoCoHaNeRe supporting this claim? And why not run BM25 negatives as a fourth strategy to close the argument empirically?
87	
88	5. **Pool size sensitivity.** How do strategy differences change as pool size increases from 50 to 200 or 500? If differences shrink at realistic pool sizes, this would substantially weaken the practical relevance of the findings.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## Minor Issues
93	
94	- Section 3.4: StarCoder2-3B is described as "Encoder-decoder" -- it is decoder-only. Correct throughout.
95	- Table 6 (stratified analysis in the best paper) vs. Table 6 (median paper): the two variants report completely different stratification schemes (by file count vs. by instance count), suggesting the analysis is not yet stable.
96	- Abstract line "SWE-bench Lite end-to-end evaluation with a Qwen3.6-27B agent" -- only Qwen retriever checkpoints are used for SWE-bench, not StarCoder. This asymmetry should be acknowledged.
97	- The paper name "StructFuse" implies a fusion system, but the best-performing approach is pure embedding mining without fusion (Table 11 shows fusion slightly degrades performance). The name is misleading.
98	- Hop depth ablation (Table 9): the "best" paper reports clean improvements (2-hop optimal), while the median paper (Table 9) reports differences "within noise range." The discrepancy in framing across tiers suggests cherry-picking of presentation.
99	- Section 3.3 reports "131 SWE-smith repositories" but only "123/131 repos producing valid output" -- the 8 failures are not analyzed.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## Overall Assessment
104	
105	This paper tackles a genuinely important question -- what makes hard negatives work for code retrieval -- with commendable experimental rigor in its design (9 seeds, bootstrap CIs, extensive ablations). The representation saturation insight, if validated on more encoders, could become a useful diagnostic tool for practitioners. However, the paper is undermined by (a) the N=2 encoder limitation that makes the "representation geometry" theory an observation rather than a validated mechanism, (b) missing baselines (BM25) that are critical to the headline narrative, (c) potential discrepancies between reported results and actual experimental maturity, (d) unrealistic pool sizes that limit external validity, and (e) several reporting gaps (no CIs on RepoBench, no stratification by structural coverage, checkpoint criterion unspecified). The paper is above-average in experimental discipline but below the bar for confident acceptance at a top venue in its current form. Addressing the BM25 baseline, the stratified analysis, and the pool size sensitivity would move it toward acceptance.
106	
107	---
108	
109	## Score: 4 / 6 (Weak Accept)
110	
111	The experimental design is sound in principle and the analytical depth is genuine, but critical baselines are missing, the mechanistic theory is underpowered (N=2), and several reporting gaps weaken trust. A revision addressing the major concerns would likely push this to a 5.
112	
113	## Confidence: 4 / 5 (High)
114	
115	I have expertise in contrastive learning, code retrieval, and hard negative mining. I have closely examined the paper's claims against the available evidence, including internal project artifacts. I am confident in my assessment of the methodological strengths and weaknesses.

The experimental design is sound in principle and the analytical depth is genuine, but critical baselines are missing, the mechanistic theory is underpowered (N=2), and several reporting gaps weaken trust. A revision addressing the major concerns would likely push this to a 5.

1. Can you provide specific passages from CoCoHaNeRe where BM25-proxy negatives are presented as embedding-distance negatives?

4. **Ablation breadth is a genuine strength.** Both credit the extensive ablation suite as above-average for this subfield.

5. **Honest reporting is commendable.** Both appreciate the paper's willingness to report null and negative results without spin.

6. **Effect sizes are too small for practical impact.** Both note that +0.5–1.3pp R@1 with no downstream significance limits the paper's practical contribution.

- **Is the "analysis paper" positioning sufficient?** R1 initially sees the ablation suite as carrying the paper; R2 argues analysis papers need deeper analytical content (connection to theory, more data points). ### Summary Judgment

The paper tackles a relevant question—what hard negative mining strategies work for code retrieval—with above-average experimental discipline. 1. **The central narrative is unsubstantiated.** The "correcting CoCoHaNeRe" motivation requires running BM25 negatives to close the argument. Without this, the paper's raison d'être is speculative.

2. **The analytical contribution is too shallow.** "Representation geometry" with n=2 encoders is an observation. Without connection to contrastive learning theory or validation across more models, it cannot stand as a primary contribution.

3. **Effect sizes are marginal.** +0.5–1.3pp R@1 with CIs including zero on one encoder, no downstream significance, and diminishing returns at larger data scales collectively suggest limited practical value.

4. **Presentation issues.** Broken bibliography ([?] throughout), StarCoder architecture mischaracterization, missing SWE-smith validation table, and inconsistent statistical reporting (CIs on SWE-bench but not RepoBench-R).

- Add 2–3 more encoders with varying pos_sim to validate the saturation hypothesis
- Provide error bars/CIs on RepoBench-R results across multiple seeds
- Fix the bibliography and the StarCoder architecture description
- Add pool-size sensitivity analysis
- Connect to hard negative theory literature (Robinson et al., Kalantidis et al.)
- Stratify dataflow results by structural data availability (34% with data vs. 66% fallback)

### Experiment Coverage vs. Design

All 13 imagined experiments are reflected in the paper: SWE-bench Lite (Tables 2–3), RepoBench-R (Table 1), repo complexity (Table 6), hop depth (Table 9), data scaling (Table 10), fusion head (Table 11), weighted vs. binary dataflow (Table 12), failure analysis (Tables 4–5), qualitative examples (§7), temperature ablation (Tables 7–8), static vs. dynamic mining (Table 13), bootstrap CIs (Table 3), and inference-time comparison (Table 14). Coverage is complete. The issue is not missing experiments but missing critical baselines (BM25) and missing statistical reporting on existing experiments (RepoBench-R CIs).

| | Score | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| R1 (Methods + Experiments) | 4/6 → 3/6 after roundtable | 4/5 |
| R2 (Novelty + Related Work) | 3/6 | 4/5 |
| **Consolidated** | **3/6 (Weak Reject)** | **4/5** |

### Decision Rationale

The paper demonstrates solid experimental practice but fails to substantiate its central narrative (CoCoHaNeRe correction without BM25 baseline), offers insufficient analytical depth for an analysis paper (representation geometry on n=2), and reports effect sizes too small for practical significance. With the suggested revisions—particularly the BM25 baseline, additional encoders, and RepoBench-R error bars—this could become a solid contribution in a future revision cycle.

### R2 adjustments after seeing R1's review:

R2 agrees that the confounded pilot-to-full comparison is the paper's most critical methodological flaw and should be elevated in importance. The inability to distinguish scale effects from distribution effects undermines the paper's central narrative.

R2 finds R1's observation about the temperature ablation (random best at τ=0.05, where hard negatives should matter most) to be an important internal contradiction that R2 had not flagged.

R2 also agrees the failure analysis backfiring (hurt 3 > helped 2) deserves more prominent framing.

**R2 maintains score at 3/6** — R1's observations reinforce rather than mitigate the weaknesses already identified.

---

## Step 3: Convergence

### Consensus Score: 3/6 (Weak Reject)

### Agreed Major Issues (ranked by severity):

1. **Confounded pilot-to-full comparison** — The paper cannot separate scale from distribution shift. This undermines the central "scale kills signal" narrative and the claimed scaling law. The subsampling experiment (Table 7) partially addresses this but draws from the full-scale distribution, not the pilot distribution.

2. **Related work critically insufficient** — 9 citations for a 10-page analysis paper at a top venue is far below expectations. Missing evaluation methodology literature (Henderson, Dodge, Bouthillier), hard negative theory (Robinson, Kalantidis), contrastive learning foundations (SimCLR, MoCo, DPR), and code representation baselines. Without positioning against existing knowledge, the paper's novelty cannot be assessed.

3. **CoCoHaNeRe critique unverified** — The paper's opening motivation asserts a flaw in CoCoHaNeRe without running a BM25 baseline to demonstrate it. The entire "correcting a misconception" framing collapses without empirical verification.

4. **"Scaling law" overstated** — 4 data points, no CIs, single encoder, no theoretical backing. Should be "trend" or "observation" with appropriate caveats.

5. **No mechanistic explanation** — The paper shows *what* (signal vanishes) but not *why* (the saturation argument doesn't explain pilot-vs-full differences). The missing neg_difficulty quartile analysis would have been the key mechanistic evidence.

6. **Presentation: 14 tables, 0 figures** — Dense, hard to skim, and fails to leverage visual communication for key findings.

### Agreed Minor Issues:

7. Two "architecturally distinct" encoders are both decoder-only transformers — overstated diversity claim.
8. Dataflow distance weighting (§6.5) deserves a table, not one sentence.
9. Qualitative examples are entirely absent.
10. Pool size of 50 never discussed; may affect strategy rankings.
11. Checkpoint selection criterion unspecified.
12. 34% structural data coverage means dataflow strategy is 2/3 random fallback — understated limitation.
13. Temperature ablation (random best even at τ=0.05) contradicts the mechanistic story but is not discussed.
14. Failure analysis shows net negative impact (hurt 3 > helped 2) for dataflow in its own target use case.

---

## Step 4: Consolidated Assessment

### Summary

This paper presents a large-scale negative result study (54 training runs) showing that hard negative mining benefits observed at pilot scale (~2K instances) for contrastive code retrieval do not replicate at full scale (15K instances, 9 seeds). The experimental effort is genuine and above field norms. The negative result itself is informative: strategy-level R@1 deltas (<1pp) are dwarfed by seed variance (~3pp), and no strategy achieves statistical significance over random sampling (bootstrap p ≥ 0.68).

### Strengths

- **Experimental scale**: 54 runs (9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders) with bootstrap CIs is well above the 1–3 seed standard in code retrieval.
- **Honest negative result reporting**: The paper does not oversell null findings and includes a thorough data pipeline audit ruling out engineering errors.
- **Comprehensive ablations**: Temperature, hop distance, fusion head, dynamic mining, distance weighting, and data size scaling are all tested and reported.
- **Scaling trend**: The observation that embedding benefit decays with data size (from +1.3pp at 1K to -0.2pp at 15K) is a concrete and useful finding, even if "scaling law" overstates it.
- **Failure taxonomy**: The manual analysis of 50 retrieval failures provides useful error categorization for the community.

### Weaknesses

- **Confounded central comparison**: The pilot-to-full transition changes both data volume and distribution. The paper's central narrative ("scale kills mining benefit") cannot be distinguished from "distribution shift kills mining benefit" without a controlled experiment.
- **Critically thin related work**: 9 citations in 3 paragraphs, missing evaluation methodology, contrastive learning theory, and code representation baselines. Novelty cannot be assessed without proper positioning.
- **Unsubstantiated motivation**: The CoCoHaNeRe critique is asserted without empirical verification (no BM25 baseline).
- **Overstated "scaling law"**: 4 data points, no confidence intervals, single encoder — should be "trend."
- **No method contribution**: Tests existing methods and finds they fail. CodeQL pipeline's value is undermined by the negative finding.
- **0 figures in 10 pages**: Dense table-only presentation fails to communicate key findings visually.
- **Missing planned experiments**: Neg_difficulty quartile analysis, qualitative examples, and tabulated distance-weighting results are absent.

### Recommendation

**Weak Reject (3/6)**. The paper demonstrates above-average experimental discipline and reports a genuine negative result, but it falls short of top-venue standards due to: (1) confounded central comparison that undermines the claimed mechanism, (2) critically insufficient related work that prevents novelty assessment, (3) unsubstantiated motivating critique of prior work, and (4) overstated "scaling law." The paper reads as a thorough project report rather than a paper with sufficient insight density for a top ML venue.

### Path to Revision

1. **Deconfound scale vs distribution**: Run a controlled experiment with pilot-distribution subsamples at increasing sizes (1K, 3K, 5K from pilot-like repos only) AND full-distribution subsamples at pilot size (2K from 123 repos). This isolates the two effects.
2. **Expand related work to 25+ citations**: Add evaluation methodology (Henderson 2018, Dodge 2019, Bouthillier 2021), hard negative theory (Robinson 2021, Kalantidis 2020), contrastive learning foundations (SimCLR, MoCo, DPR), code baselines (CodeBERT, CodeT5+, StarCoder), and structural methods (RepoGraph, RANGER).
3. **Add BM25 negative baseline**: Empirically verify the CoCoHaNeRe critique.
4. **Rename "scaling law" to "scaling trend"**: Report with CIs and cross-encoder validation.
5. **Add 3–4 key figures**: Scaling trend line plot, seed-variance box plots, failure taxonomy Sankey, stratified heatmap.
6. **Include neg_difficulty quartile analysis**: This is the missing mechanistic link.
7. **Stratify by structural data availability**: Report results separately for the 34% of instances with structural data vs the 66% without.

### Experiment Coverage Assessment

| Planned Experiment | Coverage | Notes |
|---|:-:|---|
| M2 Full Qwen 9×3 | ✅ Complete | Table 1 |
| M2 Full StarCoder 9×3 | ✅ Complete | Table 2 |
| SWE-bench Lite | ✅ Complete | Tables 3–4 |
| RepoBench-R | ✅ Complete | Table 5 |
| Stratified Analysis | ⚠️ Partial | Repo-size done (Table 8), neg_difficulty quartile missing |
| Hop-Distance Ablation | ✅ Complete | Table 12 |
| Data Size Scaling | ✅ Complete | Table 7 |
| Fusion Head Ablation | ✅ Complete | Table 13 |
| Dataflow Distance Weighting | ⚠️ Partial | One sentence in §6.5, no table |
| Failure Analysis 50 cases | ✅ Complete | Table 10 |
| Qualitative Examples | ❌ Missing | Entirely absent |
| Temperature Ablation | ✅ Complete | Table 11 |
| Dynamic vs Static Mining | ✅ Complete | Table 14 |
| Bootstrap CI SWE-bench | ✅ Complete | Table 4 |
| Inference-Time Comparison | ✅ Complete | Table 6 |
| Data Pipeline Audit | ✅ Complete | Table 9 |

**Coverage**: 12/16 complete, 2/16 partial, 1/16 missing. The missing/partial items (neg_difficulty quartile, qualitative examples, distance weighting table) would have meaningfully strengthened the analysis.

---

*Review conducted by R1 (Methods + Experiments) and R2 (Novelty + Related Work) with full roundtable protocol.*

# Dream Report Action Protocol

## Dream 审稿的特殊性

Dream 先想象三档实验数据（best/median/worst），再据此写论文，最后审稿。
审稿人看到的"实验结果"是想象的，因此审稿意见的可信度因类型而异：

### 通用建议（data-independent）— 直接可信

不管实验数据长什么样，这类意见都成立：
- 缺少某类 baseline / benchmark / 模型家族覆盖
- 引用不足或遗漏关键 related work
- 方法描述不清楚、逻辑链不完整
- framing 本身的逻辑漏洞（如 claim 之间有矛盾）
- 论文结构问题（motivation 不清、contribution 不 sharp）

### 数据依赖建议（data-dependent）— 需要跨档验证

这类意见的有效性取决于想象数据的质量：
- "claim X 太强/太弱，证据不足以支撑"
- "实验 Y 的效果不够 convincing / 缺分析"
- "表 Z 的数字不支持结论"
- "ablation 不完整，无法区分各 component 贡献"

这些可能只是因为某一档的想象数据恰好偏弱/偏强导致的。

## 分析流程

### Step 1: 提取意见列表

从三份报告中提取每条 distinct issue：

| ID | 内容摘要 | 出现档位 | 类型 |
|----|---------|---------|------|
| D1 | 缺 cross-domain baseline | [B][M][W] | 通用 |
| D2 | Claim 2 过强 | [M][W] | 数据依赖 |
| D3 | Method §3.2 描述不清 | [B] | 通用 |

注意：同一个问题用不同措辞出现在多份报告中，应合并为一条并标注所有出现档位。

### Step 2: 跨档对比判定

**通用建议**：无需跨档对比，直接评估合理性。合理的 → 确认行动项。

**数据依赖建议**——按跨档一致性判定：

| 跨档模式 | 判定 | 处理方式 |
|---------|------|---------|
| 三档一致 [B][M][W] | 结构性问题 — 不因数据好坏而改变 | → 确认行动项，立即处理 |
| 两档一致 [B][M] 或 [M][W] | 可能有效，存在不确定性 | → 观察项，记录并优先在真实实验中验证 |
| 仅单档 [B] 或 [M] 或 [W] | 很可能是想象数据的偶然产物 | → 记录但不行动，等真实实验 |

关键提醒：
- 不要因为 worst 档的想象数据差就急着"减弱 claim" — worst 本来就是最坏假设
- 不要因为 best 档的想象数据好就盲目"增强 claim" — best 本来就是最好假设
- claim 强弱的最终判断取决于真实实验，dream 只能暴露结构性问题
- **禁止因 dream 结果建议降级目标 venue** — dream 暴露的问题用"补实验/改 framing"解决，不用"换更低的会议"解决

### Step 3: 构建行动列表

**3a. 确认行动项**（即刻执行）：
- 通用建议中的合理项
- 三档一致的数据依赖建议
- 每条写明：做什么 + 改哪个文件 + 为什么

**3b. 观察项**（记录待验证）：
- 两档一致的数据依赖建议
- 单档出现但内容合理的建议
- 每条写明：观察什么指标 + 什么条件下需要行动 + 关联哪个 claim / 实验

**3c. 忽略项**（有理由地不处理）：
- 写明忽略理由

### Step 4: 持久化

1. **确认行动项** → 直接修改 `paper_framing.md` / `experiment_plan.yaml`
2. **ROADMAP 更新**：
   - 确认行动项 → "近期任务" 加 TODO
   - 观察项 → "近期任务" 加 `[Dream 观察] ...（exp-XXX 结果出来后评估）` 格式
3. **log_decision**：记录整体判断（proceed / adjust / re-dream）+ 完整分析（确认行动项 + 观察项 + 忽略项）
4. 确认行动项中涉及 framing 或 plan 改动 → 改完后**必须** re-dream 验证（`dream_simulate(review_mode="full")`），确认修改真正提升了整体质量。只有 re-dream 达标（best ≥ weak accept 且 median ≥ borderline）后才能批准 P0 实验。

### Step 5: 向 A 群汇报

**必须** `director_reply_to_user` 发送分析结论：
1. 三档评分总结
2. 必须处理的问题 + 已采取的行动
3. 记录了哪些观察项（列出具体观察点）
4. 下一步行动（改 framing? 加实验? 直接开跑 P0? re-dream?）

## 评分异常检测

如果三档评分不满足 best ≥ median ≥ worst（如 worst 评分高于 median），在汇报中
标注"评分顺序异常"，提醒用户审稿存在随机性或评分校准问题，需谨慎解读。

如果某一档标记了 `review_quality: simulated`（MCP 白名单未加载导致单 session 模拟），
该档的审稿质量降级——跨档对比时应降低其权重，必要时建议 re-dream。

## 处理态度

该处理的果断处理，模棱两可的不要硬做决定——记下来等真实实验数据出来再定。
但也不要因为"数据是想象的"就全盘忽视——通用建议和三档一致的问题是实打实的。

**行动速度**：Dream 报告分析完成后，确认行动项应**立即执行**（改 framing / 改 plan / 派 Agent 开跑）。AI 团队的优势就是从"发现问题"到"开始修复"零延迟——不要把行动项留到"下次再处理"。

content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_5/projects/structfuse-context/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — StructFuse\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main\\n- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026\\n\\n## Core Claims (3)\\n\\n1. **True embedding-distance hard negative mining consistently improves contrastive code retrieval over random baselines, correcting the prior misconception that embedding negatives harm performance.** The reported \\\"harm\\\" (CoCoHaNeRe-derived, -27pp R@1) was an artifact of BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance — genuine embedding mining yields +1.6–2.0pp R@1 across two architecturally distinct encoders (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B).\\n\\n2. **Structure-grounded (dataflow) hard negatives provide conditional additional benefit beyond embedding mining, mediated by encoder representation saturation.** When pretrained encoder representations are compressed (pos_sim > 0.98, as in Qwen), random and embedding negatives become too easy; dataflow-disconnected negatives force discrimination along a structural dimension the encoder cannot separate via text alone. When representation space is healthy (pos_sim ~ 0.80, as in StarCoder), embedding mining alone suffices. Mechanism: neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) provides quantitative evidence for this interaction.\\n\\n3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL is a scalable, model-independent method for computing structural connectivity.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. Method is a general-purpose structural negative generator applicable beyond code (molecular networks, circuit topology, KG retrieval).\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.\\n\\n- **Existing approaches & gaps**:\\n  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies\\n  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal\\n  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only\\n  - CoCoHaNeRe: reports embedding negatives harm code search — but uses BM25 proxy, not true embedding distance\\n  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works\\n\\n- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. We (1) correct the misconception that embedding negatives harm performance (BM25 proxy ≠ embedding distance), (2) introduce structure-grounded negatives via inter-procedural dataflow and characterize when they provide additional benefit, and (3) provide mechanistic explanation via representation space saturation analysis.\\n\\n- **Headline result template**: \\\"True embedding-distance mining consistently improves code retrieval (+1.6–2.0pp R@1, 2 encoders), correcting prior reports of harm. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives provide further conditional benefit (+0.8–2.3pp) when encoder representations are saturated, with the interaction mechanism quantified via negative difficulty analysis.\\\"\\n\\n## Core Insight\\n\\nThe effectiveness of hard negative mining strategies depends on the encoder's representation geometry. When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction explains contradictory findings in prior work.\\n\\n## Dual-Pillar Motivation\\n\\n1. **Primary — Systematic analysis correcting misconceptions**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe) conflated BM25-proxy negatives with true embedding-distance negatives, leading to incorrect conclusions about hard negative mining for code. Our controlled comparison isolates the effect of each strategy.\\n2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) provides explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, enabling practitioners to predict which strategy suits their encoder without exhaustive experiments.\\n\\n## Formal Definition\\n\\nGiven retrieval domain D, structural graph G, similarity function s, query q:\\n**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : s(x,q) > τ ∧ ¬reachable_G(x,q)} s(x,q)\\n\\nThe structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune).\\n\\n## Title Options\\n\\n- Primary: \\\"What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? A Systematic Study of Mining Strategies and Representation Geometry\\\"\\n- Alternative: \\\"StructFuse: When and Why Structure-Grounded Hard Negatives Improve Contrastive Code Retrieval\\\"\\n- Backup: \\\"Correcting Misconceptions in Hard Negative Mining for Code: Embedding Distance Helps, Structure Helps Conditionally\\\"\\n\\n## Venue Fit\\n\\n1. **EMNLP Main fit**: Empirical analysis + mechanistic insight papers are a strong EMNLP archetype (cf. \\\"Do Language Models...\\\" papers). Contribution is understanding, not just a new method.\\n2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.\\n3. **Against \\\"incremental\\\" criticism**: Paper corrects a misconception + provides mechanistic explanation + introduces new negative mining paradigm. Three contributions, not one marginal improvement.\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns\\n\\n| Concern | Response | Evidence |\\n|---------|----------|----------|\\n| Only 2 encoders — can you generalize? | n=2 is minimum for interaction claim; we frame as observation with mechanism, not universal law; cross-architecture (decoder vs encoder-decoder) strengthens it | plan_013 (done), m2_full runs |\\n| Temperature regime specificity | Ablate τ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} | plan_014 |\\n| No downstream task evaluation | SWE-bench Lite end-to-end with LLM agent | plan_003 |\\n| Static vs dynamic mining confound | Clarify mining is static; add dynamic baseline | plan_015 |\\n| CodeQL scalability at larger scale | 0% timeout, 78% Z%, 123 repos; m1_reextract_v2 adds more | plan_006 (done) |\\n| Why not compare inference-time graph methods? | Complementary: they navigate at inference, we mine at training. Discuss relationship. | plan_017 |\\n| Single benchmark | Add RepoBench-R cross-file retrieval | plan_004 |\\n| Statistical significance | Bootstrap 95% CI for all comparisons; full M2 = 9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders | plan_016, m2_full |\\n| \\\"Complementary signal\\\" overstatement | Temper: \\\"conditionally beneficial\\\" not \\\"always complementary\\\" | Writing discipline |\\n| Missing related work | RepoFusion, GRACE, GraphCodeBERT, ANCE, curriculum HN mining | Writing task |\\n\\n## Evidence Status\\n\\n### Confirmed findings (basis for claims):\\n- D017: True embedding mining helps (+2.0pp Qwen, +1.6pp StarCoder) — corrects MVP BM25-proxy artifact\\n- D021/neg_difficulty: Qwen pos_sim=0.9855 (saturated), StarCoder pos_sim=0.7985 (healthy); margin differential explains strategy interaction\\n- m2_embed_verify (pilot): 3-strategy comparison confirms ranking (embedding > random, dataflow conditional)\\n- plan_013 (StarCoder pilot): Confirms cross-encoder pattern — embedding helps both, dataflow helps Qwen only\\n- plan_006: CodeQL scalability confirmed at 123-repo scale\\n\\n### In progress:\\n- m2_full_qwen: 9 seeds × 3 strategies (seed 1 running, best R@1=55.3% at step 1000)\\n- m2_full_starcoder: 9 seeds × 3 strategies (seed 1 running, R@1=45.4% at step 1000, still improving)\\n- m1_reextract_v2: expanded extraction for higher coverage\\n\\n### Planned (priority order):\\n- plan_003: SWE-bench Lite eval (biggest lever for paper strength)\\n- plan_014: Temperature ablation (Dream reviewer concern)\\n- plan_004: RepoBench-R second benchmark\\n- plan_015: Dynamic mining baseline\\n- plan_007/008/009: Additional ablations\\n\\n## Contingency (if full M2 results weaken claims)\\n\\n### All 18 runs confirm pilot pattern: Best case\\n- Full statistical power, paper as framed above\\n- Target: EMNLP Main\\n\\n### Dataflow benefit disappears even for Qwen at full scale: Pivot to 2-claim paper\\n- Drop Claim 2 to analysis observation\\n- Paper becomes: \\\"True embedding mining helps (correcting misconception) + CodeQL extraction is practical + representation geometry analysis explains prior contradictions\\\"\\n- Still publishable: correcting misconception + mechanistic analysis is sufficient for EMNLP Main\\n\\n### Embedding mining also loses advantage at full scale: Major reassessment needed\\n- Recheck data pipeline for bugs (full-scale data may have distribution differences)\\n- If confirmed: negative result paper — \\\"Why Hard Negative Mining Doesn't Scale for Code Retrieval\\\"\\n- Discuss with user before committing direction\\n\\n## Deprecated Claims (with reason)\\n\\n- ~~\\\"Embedding-distance hard negatives actively harm code retrieval\\\"~~ — FALSIFIED by D017. Original evidence (-27pp R@1) was from BM25-proxy negatives incorrectly labeled as embedding_distance in MVP. True embedding mining shows consistent improvement. Preserved here to prevent regression.\\n\", \"total_chars\": 9391, \"truncated\": false}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {}}"}

## Target Venue
- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main
- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026

## Core Claims (3)

1. **True embedding-distance hard negative mining consistently improves contrastive code retrieval over random baselines, correcting the prior misconception that embedding negatives harm performance.** The reported "harm" (CoCoHaNeRe-derived, -27pp R@1) was an artifact of BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance — genuine embedding mining yields +1.6–2.0pp R@1 across two architecturally distinct encoders (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B).

2. **Structure-grounded (dataflow) hard negatives provide conditional additional benefit beyond embedding mining, mediated by encoder representation saturation.** When pretrained encoder representations are compressed (pos_sim > 0.98, as in Qwen), random and embedding negatives become too easy; dataflow-disconnected negatives force discrimination along a structural dimension the encoder cannot separate via text alone. When representation space is healthy (pos_sim ~ 0.80, as in StarCoder), embedding mining alone suffices. Mechanism: neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) provides quantitative evidence for this interaction.

3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL is a scalable, model-independent method for computing structural connectivity.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. Method is a general-purpose structural negative generator applicable beyond code (molecular networks, circuit topology, KG retrieval).

## Story Spine

- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.

- **Existing approaches & gaps**:
  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies
  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal
  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only
  - CoCoHaNeRe: reports embedding negatives harm code search — but uses BM25 proxy, not true embedding distance
  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works

- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. We (1) correct the misconception that embedding negatives harm performance (BM25 proxy ≠ embedding distance), (2) introduce structure-grounded negatives via inter-procedural dataflow and characterize when they provide additional benefit, and (3) provide mechanistic explanation via representation space saturation analysis.

- **Headline result template**: "True embedding-distance mining consistently improves code retrieval (+1.6–2.0pp R@1, 2 encoders), correcting prior reports of harm. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives provide further conditional benefit (+0.8–2.3pp) when encoder representations are saturated, with the interaction mechanism quantified via negative difficulty analysis."

## Core Insight

The effectiveness of hard negative mining strategies depends on the encoder's representation geometry. When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction explains contradictory findings in prior work.

## Dual-Pillar Motivation

1. **Primary — Systematic analysis correcting misconceptions**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe) conflated BM25-proxy negatives with true embedding-distance negatives, leading to incorrect conclusions about hard negative mining for code. Our controlled comparison isolates the effect of each strategy.
2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) provides explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, enabling practitioners to predict which strategy suits their encoder without exhaustive experiments.

## Formal Definition

Given retrieval domain D, structural graph G, similarity function s, query q:
**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : s(x,q) > τ ∧ ¬reachable_G(x,q)} s(x,q)

The structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune).

## Title Options

- Primary: "What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? A Systematic Study of Mining Strategies and Representation Geometry"
- Alternative: "StructFuse: When and Why Structure-Grounded Hard Negatives Improve Contrastive Code Retrieval"
- Backup: "Correcting Misconceptions in Hard Negative Mining for Code: Embedding Distance Helps, Structure Helps Conditionally"

## Venue Fit

1. **EMNLP Main fit**: Empirical analysis + mechanistic insight papers are a strong EMNLP archetype (cf. "Do Language Models..." papers). Contribution is understanding, not just a new method.
2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.
3. **Against "incremental" criticism**: Paper corrects a misconception + provides mechanistic explanation + introduces new negative mining paradigm. Three contributions, not one marginal improvement.

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

| Concern | Response | Evidence |

| Missing related work | RepoFusion, GRACE, GraphCodeBERT, ANCE, curriculum HN mining | Writing task |

content.content:
1	# Paper Framing — StructFuse
2	
3	## Target Venue
4	- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main
5	- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026
6	
7	## Core Claims (3)
8	
9	1. **True embedding-distance hard negative mining consistently improves contrastive code retrieval over random baselines, correcting the prior misconception that embedding negatives harm performance.** The reported "harm" (CoCoHaNeRe-derived, -27pp R@1) was an artifact of BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance — genuine embedding mining yields +1.6–2.0pp R@1 across two architecturally distinct encoders (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B).
10	
11	2. **Structure-grounded (dataflow) hard negatives provide conditional additional benefit beyond embedding mining, mediated by encoder representation saturation.** When pretrained encoder representations are compressed (pos_sim > 0.98, as in Qwen), random and embedding negatives become too easy; dataflow-disconnected negatives force discrimination along a structural dimension the encoder cannot separate via text alone. When representation space is healthy (pos_sim ~ 0.80, as in StarCoder), embedding mining alone suffices. Mechanism: neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) provides quantitative evidence for this interaction.
12	
13	3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL is a scalable, model-independent method for computing structural connectivity.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. Method is a general-purpose structural negative generator applicable beyond code (molecular networks, circuit topology, KG retrieval).
14	
15	## Story Spine
16	
17	- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.
18	
19	- **Existing approaches & gaps**:
20	  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies
21	  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal
22	  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only
23	  - CoCoHaNeRe: reports embedding negatives harm code search — but uses BM25 proxy, not true embedding distance
24	  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works

# Paper Framing — StructFuse

## Target Venue
- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main
- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026

## Core Claims (3)

1. **True embedding-distance hard negative mining consistently improves contrastive code retrieval over random baselines, correcting the prior misconception that embedding negatives harm performance.** The reported "harm" (CoCoHaNeRe-derived, -27pp R@1) was an artifact of BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance — genuine embedding mining yields +1.6–2.0pp R@1 across two architecturally distinct encoders (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B).

2. **Structure-grounded (dataflow) hard negatives provide conditional additional benefit beyond embedding mining, mediated by encoder representation saturation.** When pretrained encoder representations are compressed (pos_sim > 0.98, as in Qwen), random and embedding negatives become too easy; dataflow-disconnected negatives force discrimination along a structural dimension the encoder cannot separate via text alone. When representation space is healthy (pos_sim ~ 0.80, as in StarCoder), embedding mining alone suffices. Mechanism: neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) provides quantitative evidence for this interaction.

3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL is a scalable, model-independent method for computing structural connectivity.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. Method is a general-purpose structural negative generator applicable beyond code (molecular networks, circuit topology, KG retrieval).

## Story Spine

- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.

- **Existing approaches & gaps**:
  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies
  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal
  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only
  - CoCoHaNeRe: reports embedding negatives harm code search — but uses BM25 proxy, not true embedding distance
  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works

- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. We (1) correct the misconception that embedding negatives harm performance (BM25 proxy ≠ embedding distance), (2) introduce structure-grounded negatives via inter-procedural dataflow and characterize when they provide additional benefit, and (3) provide mechanistic explanation via representation space saturation analysis.

- **Headline result template**: "True embedding-distance mining consistently improves code retrieval (+1.6–2.0pp R@1, 2 encoders), correcting prior reports of harm. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives provide further conditional benefit (+0.8–2.3pp) when encoder representations are saturated, with the interaction mechanism quantified via negative difficulty analysis."

## Core Insight

The effectiveness of hard negative mining strategies depends on the encoder's representation geometry. When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction explains contradictory findings in prior work.

## Dual-Pillar Motivation

1. **Primary — Systematic analysis correcting misconceptions**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe) conflated BM25-proxy negatives with true embedding-distance negatives, leading to incorrect conclusions about hard negative mining for code. Our controlled comparison isolates the effect of each strategy.
2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) provides explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, enabling practitioners to predict which strategy suits their encoder without exhaustive experiments.

## Formal Definition

Given retrieval domain D, structural graph G, similarity function s, query q:
**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : s(x,q) > τ ∧ ¬reachable_G(x,q)} s(x,q)

The structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune).

## Title Options

- Primary: "What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? A Systematic Study of Mining Strategies and Representation Geometry"
- Alternative: "StructFuse: When and Why Structure-Grounded Hard Negatives Improve Contrastive Code Retrieval"
- Backup: "Correcting Misconceptions in Hard Negative Mining for Code: Embedding Distance Helps, Structure Helps Conditionally"

## Venue Fit

1. **EMNLP Main fit**: Empirical analysis + mechanistic insight papers are a strong EMNLP archetype (cf. "Do Language Models..." papers). Contribution is understanding, not just a new method.
2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.
3. **Against "incremental" criticism**: Paper corrects a misconception + provides mechanistic explanation + introduces new negative mining paradigm. Three contributions, not one marginal improvement.

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

| Concern | Response | Evidence |
|---------|----------|----------|
| Only 2 encoders — can you generalize? | n=2 is minimum for interaction claim; we frame as observation with mechanism, not universal law; cross-architecture (decoder vs encoder-decoder) strengthens it | plan_013 (done), m2_full runs |
| Temperature regime specificity | Ablate τ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} | plan_014 |
| No downstream task evaluation | SWE-bench Lite end-to-end with LLM agent | plan_003 |
| Static vs dynamic mining confound | Clarify mining is static; add dynamic baseline | plan_015 |
| CodeQL scalability at larger scale | 0% timeout, 78% Z%, 123 repos; m1_reextract_v2 adds more | plan_006 (done) |
| Why not compare inference-time graph methods? | Complementary: they navigate at inference, we mine at training. Discuss relationship. | plan_017 |
| Single benchmark | Add RepoBench-R cross-file retrieval | plan_004 |
| Statistical significance | Bootstrap 95% CI for all comparisons; full M2 = 9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders | plan_016, m2_full |
| "Complementary signal" overstatement | Temper: "conditionally beneficial" not "always complementary" | Writing discipline |
| Missing related work | RepoFusion, GRACE, GraphCodeBERT, ANCE, curriculum HN mining | Writing task |

## Evidence Status

### Confirmed findings (basis for claims):
- D017: True embedding mining helps (+2.0pp Qwen, +1.6pp StarCoder) — corrects MVP BM25-proxy artifact
- D021/neg_difficulty: Qwen pos_sim=0.9855 (saturated), StarCoder pos_sim=0.7985 (healthy); margin differential explains strategy interaction
- m2_embed_verify (pilot): 3-strategy comparison confirms ranking (embedding > random, dataflow conditional)
- plan_013 (StarCoder pilot): Confirms cross-encoder pattern — embedding helps both, dataflow helps Qwen only
- plan_006: CodeQL scalability confirmed at 123-repo scale

### In progress:
- m2_full_qwen: 9 seeds × 3 strategies (seed 1 running, best R@1=55.3% at step 1000)
- m2_full_starcoder: 9 seeds × 3 strategies (seed 1 running, R@1=45.4% at step 1000, still improving)
- m1_reextract_v2: expanded extraction for higher coverage

### Planned (priority order):
- plan_003: SWE-bench Lite eval (biggest lever for paper strength)
- plan_014: Temperature ablation (Dream reviewer concern)
- plan_004: RepoBench-R second benchmark
- plan_015: Dynamic mining baseline
- plan_007/008/009: Additional ablations

## Contingency (if full M2 results weaken claims)

### All 18 runs confirm pilot pattern: Best case
- Full statistical power, paper as framed above
- Target: EMNLP Main

### Dataflow benefit disappears even for Qwen at full scale: Pivot to 2-claim paper
- Drop Claim 2 to analysis observation
- Paper becomes: "True embedding mining helps (correcting misconception) + CodeQL extraction is practical + representation geometry analysis explains prior contradictions"
- Still publishable: correcting misconception + mechanistic analysis is sufficient for EMNLP Main

### Embedding mining also loses advantage at full scale: Major reassessment needed
- Recheck data pipeline for bugs (full-scale data may have distribution differences)
- If confirmed: negative result paper — "Why Hard Negative Mining Doesn't Scale for Code Retrieval"
- Discuss with user before committing direction

## Deprecated Claims (with reason)

- ~~"Embedding-distance hard negatives actively harm code retrieval"~~ — FALSIFIED by D017. Original evidence (-27pp R@1) was from BM25-proxy negatives incorrectly labeled as embedding_distance in MVP. True embedding mining shows consistent improvement. Preserved here to prevent regression.

# StructFuse — Research Dashboard

## 核心方向
True embedding-distance mining consistently improves contrastive code retrieval (+1.6–2.0pp R@1), correcting prior misconceptions that embedding negatives harm performance. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives provide conditional additional benefit mediated by encoder representation saturation. 详见 paper_framing.md。

## 当前进展
- **阶段**: Research（post-MVP）+ 审稿进行中
- **M2 全量训练**: 18 runs 全覆盖（Qwen 9 + StarCoder 9），链式自动执行
  - Qwen: random_s42 done, random_s43 running, 全 9 runs ETA ~May 19
  - StarCoder: random_s42 running (~87%), 全 9 runs ETA ~May 20
- **Dream full review 完成 (D029)**: Best 4/6 WA, Median 3/6 WR, Worst 3/6 WR
  - #1 结构性问题: 缺 BM25 baseline → 已加 plan_018 P0
  - 已修正: StarCoder 架构描述、RepoBench-R 多 seed CI、pool size sensitivity、structural coverage 分层
- **评估脚本就绪**: SWE-bench Lite (plan_003) + RepoBench-R (plan_004)
- **m1_reextract_v2**: 后台进行 (71/82 groups)

## 近期任务
- [ ] **plan_018 BM25 mining Phase 1 (CPU)** — 立即开始，与 M2 并行
- [ ] M2 full 18 runs 完成（Qwen ~May 19, StarCoder ~May 20）
- [ ] 统计检验 (bootstrap CI, paired t-test) — M2 完成后立即
- [ ] plan_003 SWE-bench Lite eval — M2 Qwen best checkpoint ready 后
- [ ] plan_004 RepoBench-R (多 seed + CIs)
- [ ] plan_018 Phase 2 (GPU training) — M2 释放 GPU 后
- [ ] plan_019 pool size sensitivity — M2 checkpoints ready 后
- [ ] plan_014 temperature ablation — GPU 空出后
- [ ] plan_005 stratified analysis (含 structural coverage 分层)
- [ ] [Dream 观察] effect sizes — M2 真实数据出来后评估是否 <1pp
- [ ] [Dream 观察] overfitting learning curves — 提取现有训练 log
- [ ] 论文初稿 (~May 24)

## Go/No-Go 阈值 (D019/D020, 适配 D024)
**Claim 1 (embedding vs random)**: 预期 Go — pilot 已一致确认。Full M2 提供 3-seed CI。
**Claim 2 (dataflow conditional)**: Conditional Go — 等 M2 统计结果 (D028)。
**BM25 baseline (plan_018)**: 必须完成 — Dream #1 共识，纸面叙事依赖此实证。

## GPU 预算
- **bjb1-42106**: 2× RTX PRO 6000 96GB（专属），满载
  - cuda:0: m2_full_qwen (training, registry 显示 ANALYZING 但实际在跑)
  - cuda:1: m2_full_starcoder (RUNNING)
- **剩余**: ~120 GPU-h needed (plan_018:15h + plan_003:40h + plan_014:35h + plan_004:15h + plan_019:5h + 余量)
- **关键路径**: M2(~May 19-20) → 统计+plan_018 Phase 2(~May 21) → plan_003(~May 22) → 初稿(~May 24) → ARR May 25

## 关键风险
1. **ARR deadline May 25**: 5 天内完成 M2→统计→eval→BM25→初稿，紧但可行（AI 团队速度）
2. **BM25 baseline 新增**: plan_018 Phase 2 需 ~15 GPU-h，与 plan_003/014 争 GPU
3. **n=3 统计功效**: df=2 Type II error 高，Discussion 必须讨论

1	# Paper Framing — StructFuse
2	
3	## Target Venue
4	- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main
5	- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026
6	
7	## Core Claims (3)
8	
9	1. **True embedding-distance hard negative mining consistently improves contrastive code retrieval over random baselines, correcting the prior misconception that embedding negatives harm performance.** The reported "harm" (CoCoHaNeRe-derived, -27pp R@1) was an artifact of BM25-proxy negatives mislabeled as embedding-distance — genuine embedding mining yields +1.6–2.0pp R@1 across two decoder-only encoders with distinct pretraining corpora and representation geometries (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B).
10	
11	2. **Structure-grounded (dataflow) hard negatives provide conditional additional benefit beyond embedding mining, mediated by encoder representation saturation.** When pretrained encoder representations are compressed (pos_sim > 0.98, as in Qwen), random and embedding negatives become too easy; dataflow-disconnected negatives force discrimination along a structural dimension the encoder cannot separate via text alone. When representation space is healthy (pos_sim ~ 0.80, as in StarCoder), embedding mining alone suffices. Mechanism: neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) provides quantitative evidence for this interaction.
12	
13	3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL provides a practical pipeline for computing structural connectivity at scale.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. [Dream [M][W] flag: this is supporting methodology, not a primary research contribution. Drop speculative generalization claims (molecular networks, etc.) — no evidence. Frame as practical tool that enables the study, not a standalone contribution.]
14	
15	## Story Spine
16	
17	- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.
18	
19	- **Existing approaches & gaps**:
20	  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies
21	  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal
22	  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only
23	  - CoCoHaNeRe: reports embedding negatives harm code search — but uses BM25 proxy, not true embedding distance
24	  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works
25	
26	- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. We (1) correct the misconception that embedding negatives harm performance (BM25 proxy ≠ embedding distance), (2) introduce structure-grounded negatives via inter-procedural dataflow and characterize when they provide additional benefit, and (3) provide mechanistic explanation via representation space saturation analysis.
27	
28	- **Headline result template**: "True embedding-distance mining consistently improves code retrieval (+1.6–2.0pp R@1, 2 encoders), correcting prior reports of harm. Structure-grounded (dataflow) negatives provide further conditional benefit (+0.8–2.3pp) when encoder representations are saturated, with the interaction mechanism quantified via negative difficulty analysis."
29	
30	## Core Insight
31	
32	The effectiveness of hard negative mining strategies depends on the encoder's representation geometry. When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction explains contradictory findings in prior work.
33	
34	## Dual-Pillar Motivation
35	
36	1. **Primary — Systematic analysis correcting misconceptions**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe) conflated BM25-proxy negatives with true embedding-distance negatives, leading to incorrect conclusions about hard negative mining for code. Our controlled comparison isolates the effect of each strategy.
37	2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) provides explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, enabling practitioners to predict which strategy suits their encoder without exhaustive experiments.
38	
39	## Formal Definition
40	
41	Given retrieval domain D, structural graph G, similarity function s, query q:
42	**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : s(x,q) > τ ∧ ¬reachable_G(x,q)} s(x,q)
43	
44	The structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune).
45	
46	## Title Options
47	
48	- Primary: "What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? A Systematic Study of Mining Strategies and Representation Geometry"
49	- Alternative: "StructFuse: When and Why Structure-Grounded Hard Negatives Improve Contrastive Code Retrieval"
50	- Backup: "Correcting Misconceptions in Hard Negative Mining for Code: Embedding Distance Helps, Structure Helps Conditionally"
51	
52	## Venue Fit
53	
54	1. **EMNLP Main fit**: Empirical analysis + mechanistic insight papers are a strong EMNLP archetype (cf. "Do Language Models..." papers). Contribution is understanding, not just a new method.
55	2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.
56	3. **Against "incremental" criticism**: Paper corrects a misconception + provides mechanistic explanation + introduces new negative mining paradigm. Three contributions, not one marginal improvement.
57	
58	## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns
59	
60	| Concern | Response | Evidence |
61	|---------|----------|----------|
62	| Only 2 encoders — can you generalize? | n=2 is minimum for interaction claim; we frame as observation with mechanism, not universal law; two decoder-only encoders with distinct pretraining (Fill vs FIM) and representation geometry (pos_sim 0.99 vs 0.80) provide meaningful variation | plan_013 (done), m2_full runs |
63	| BM25 vs true embedding negatives? | Run BM25 negatives to empirically verify CoCoHaNeRe used BM25-proxy, closing the correction argument | plan_018 |
64	| Pool size sensitivity? | Evaluate at pool {50, 100, 200, 500} to confirm strategy rankings hold at realistic sizes | plan_019 |
65	| Stratified by structural data availability? | Report per-stratum R@1 for 34% with structural data vs 66% fallback | plan_005 (extended) |
66	| Temperature regime specificity | Ablate τ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} | plan_014 |
67	| No downstream task evaluation | SWE-bench Lite end-to-end with LLM agent | plan_003 |
68	| Static vs dynamic mining confound | Clarify mining is static; add dynamic baseline | plan_015 |
69	| CodeQL scalability at larger scale | 0% timeout, 78% Z%, 123 repos; m1_reextract_v2 adds more | plan_006 (done) |
70	| Why not compare inference-time graph methods? | Complementary: they navigate at inference, we mine at training. Discuss relationship. | plan_017 |
71	| Single benchmark | Add RepoBench-R cross-file retrieval | plan_004 |
72	| Statistical significance | Bootstrap 95% CI for all comparisons; full M2 = 9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders | plan_016, m2_full |
73	| "Complementary signal" overstatement | Temper: "conditionally beneficial" not "always complementary" | Writing discipline |
74	| Missing related work | RepoFusion, GRACE, GraphCodeBERT, ANCE, curriculum HN mining | Writing task |
75	
76	## Evidence Status
77	
78	### Confirmed findings (basis for claims):
79	- D017: True embedding mining helps (+2.0pp Qwen, +1.6pp StarCoder) — corrects MVP BM25-proxy artifact
